name: Cholesterol
lead: Cholesterol is the main sterol in animals: a structural component of cell membranes and a precursor to steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D. Nearly all animal cells can make it, with the liver and intestines producing about 80 percent of the daily total.[1]

In skin, cholesterol is one of three main lipids in the stratum corneum, alongside ceramides and free fatty acids. Wikipedia describes this matrix as the 'mortar' that limits water loss, and gives a rough weight ratio of about 50 percent ceramides, 25 percent cholesterol and 15 percent free fatty acids.[1] Barrier-repair moisturisers sometimes include cholesterol with ceramides for this reason.

In looksmaxxing discussion cholesterol also arises in diet and testosterone debates, where blood levels are weighed against cardiovascular risk. Clinical guidelines such as the NCEP Adult Treatment Panel III address blood cholesterol and heart disease.[2]
infobox: Membrane component; precursor of steroid hormones, bile acids, vitamin D
Barrier lipid alongside ceramides and fatty acids

paras: Synthesis takes roughly 37 steps from acetyl-CoA, with HMG-CoA reductase as the rate-limiting enzyme and the target of statins. The SREBP pathway senses cellular cholesterol and adjusts production.[1] Cholesterol is also central to membrane organisation, including lipid rafts.[3]

The outer skin layer relies on an ordered lipid mixture of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids to retain water, per Wikipedia.[1] Cosmetic use of topical cholesterol is not covered by that article, and the sources reviewed do not include trials of cholesterol-containing moisturisers for appearance.

Elevated LDL cholesterol is associated with atherosclerosis, heart attack and stroke, while HDL is thought to carry cholesterol back to the liver. Treatments include diet changes, statins and other lipid-lowering drugs; about 1 in 250 people have familial hypercholesterolaemia.[1] The NCEP ATP III guideline is a landmark framework for detecting and treating high blood cholesterol in adults.[2]

Francois Poulletier de la Salle identified cholesterol in gallstones in 1769, and Michel Eugene Chevreul named it cholesterine in 1815. Konrad Bloch and Feodor Lynen shared the 1964 Nobel Prize for work on cholesterol and fatty-acid metabolism, and Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein won in 1985 for the SREBP regulatory pathway.[1]

No studies found on topical cholesterol for skin appearance. Human research on cholesterol is extensive for cardiovascular risk, for example guideline work and large risk-prediction studies such as the Framingham cohort,[2][4] and registered trials address Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, a cholesterol-synthesis disorder.[5]

card.summary: The body's key membrane sterol and a third of the skin's barrier lipid mix; in skincare it shows up alongside ceramides, with no appearance trials on its own.
card.note: Blood cholesterol and topical cholesterol are different topics; heart-health guidance concerns the former.

quick.overview:
Cholesterol is a waxy lipid every animal cell uses. In skin it forms part of the lipid mortar, with ceramides and fatty acids, that holds water in.

Barrier-repair creams sometimes include it for that reason, but the sources reviewed contain no appearance trials of topical cholesterol.
quick.mechanism: In the stratum corneum it packs with ceramides and fatty acids into ordered layers that limit water loss. In the body it is a precursor to hormones, bile acids and vitamin D.
quick.risks: High blood LDL cholesterol is linked to heart disease and is treated under clinical guidelines. Topical cosmetic use was not assessed in the sources reviewed.
